title: p-Block Elements: Group 13 & 14
tagline: Boron, aluminium, carbon and silicon: inert pairs, carbides and the semiconductors.

overview.intro: The p-block of periods 2 and 3 contains the elements that build both organic chemistry and modern electronics. This chapter covers group 13, where boron behaves as a non-metal forming electron-deficient compounds and aluminium shows the inert-pair effect and diagonal relationship, and group 14, where carbon’s catenation underlies all of chemistry and silicon supplies the network solids and semiconductors. The examination favours the anomalies: why boron cannot form BF6^3−, why the +1 state grows more stable down group 13, and how a semiconductor’s conductivity changes with temperature.

facts.label: Group 13
facts.value: B, Al, Ga, In, Tl: ns^2 np^1; +3 common, +1 increasingly stable down the group.

facts.label: Group 14
facts.value: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb: ns^2 np^2; catenation strongest in carbon.

facts.label: Semiconductors
facts.value: Si and Ge have conductivity between metals and insulators, rising with temperature.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Boron hydrides, the inert-pair effect and semiconductor reasoning carry the marks.

learningOutcomes: Describe the electronic configuration and oxidation states of group 13 and group 14 elements.
Explain the inert-pair effect and predict the stable oxidation state of a named heavy member.
Describe the structure and bonding of boron trifluoride, diborane and aluminium chloride.
Compare the structures of diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide, and relate them to properties.
Explain p-type and n-type semiconductor behaviour and the use of germanium in electronics.

blocks.text: Boron and aluminium share the configuration ns^2 np^1 and the common +3 oxidation state, but they sit either side of the metal–non-metal line. Boron is a metalloid: it forms covalent compounds only, never a B3+ ion, because the small triply charged ion would need an impossibly large hydration or lattice energy. Its most famous compound, boron trifluoride, has only six electrons around boron, so it accepts a lone pair and acts as a strong Lewis acid, forming adducts with ammonia and ether. Aluminium is a metal that dissolves in both acids and alkali, giving the aluminate ion in base, and its chloride is covalent and dimeric because Al3+ polarises the chloride ion strongly. Down the group the +1 state becomes progressively more stable, particularly for thallium, because the 6s^2 pair is held so close to the nucleus by poor shielding that it refuses to take part in bonding.

items: Boron never forms BF6^3−: there is no low-energy d orbital on boron to expand its octet.
BF3 is a Lewis acid because boron has only six valence electrons.
Al2O3 is amphoteric, dissolving in both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
AlCl3 dimerises to Al2Cl6 through coordinate bonds, each aluminium completing its octet.
Inert-pair effect: TlCl is more stable than TlCl3 because the 6s^2 pair stays inert.
Boron forms three-centre two-electron bonds in diborane, which is electron-deficient.

items.note: Boron accepts nitrogen’s lone pair to complete its octet, showing classic Lewis acidity.

items.text: Aluminium dissolved in excess sodium hydroxide

blocks.text: Group 14 elements have four valence electrons and so can form four bonds, and carbon takes this further than any other element because of two properties: its small size gives strong short bonds, and the C–C bond is almost as strong as the C–H bond, so long chains and rings form readily. This catenation declines sharply down the group, which is why silicon chains beyond a few atoms are unstable while carbon chemistry fills the world. Carbon shows oxidation states from −4 to +4 and forms the giant covalent network of diamond, the layered structure of graphite and the fullerenes; silicon shows only +4 and −4 practically, and its chemistry is dominated by the Si–O bond, which is strong enough to make silicates the most abundant minerals. The inert-pair effect again appears at the bottom: lead(IV) is a strong oxidant and lead(II) the stable state, which is why lead dioxide oxidises hydrochloric acid to chlorine.

items: Diamond: every carbon sp^3 bonded to four others in a rigid tetrahedral network, very hard and non-conducting.
Graphite: layers of sp^2 carbon with delocalised electrons, soft, slippery and conducting.
Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent lattice with each silicon bonded to four oxygens, melting only above 1600 °C.
Silicates are SiO4^4− tetrahedra sharing one, two, three or four oxygens to give discrete, chain, sheet and framework structures.
Lead(IV) oxide oxidises concentrated hydrochloric acid because Pb–Cl bonding is weak once the inert pair is involved.
Fullerenes such as C60 are closed cages of pentagons and hexagons.

items.note: Only a substance of similar hardness can scratch a giant covalent network.
Lead(IV) is reduced to lead(II), showing that the +2 state is the stable one for lead.

items.meaning: Ability of an element to form bonds with atoms of the same element, forming chains.
Lower reactivity of the outer s electrons in heavier p-block elements.
Substance with conductivity between that of a metal and an insulator.
Compound built from SiO4^4− tetrahedra sharing corner oxygens.

learn.title: Compounds: boric acid, borax and the alums

blocks.text: Boric acid, H3BO3, is a planar molecule that hydrogen-bonds into sheets, giving it a soapy feel and making it only slightly soluble in cold water. It behaves not as a proton donor but as a Lewis acid: it accepts hydroxide from water and releases a proton, which is why its basicity increases on dilution. Borax, Na2B4O7·10H2O, is the source of the borate ions used in the bead test and in soaps; when dissolved it hydrolyses to give an alkaline solution of boric acid and sodium metaborate, forming a buffer near pH 9.2. Aluminium sulfate finds its uses through the alums, double salts of formula K2SO4·Al2(SO4)3·24H2O whose large, hydrated crystals are used in water purification and in dyeing: the aluminium ion hydrolyses to give a gelatinous aluminium hydroxide that adsorbs suspended particles and carries them down.

items: Boric acid is a weak monobasic Lewis acid: B(OH)3 + 2H2O ⇌ [B(OH)4]− + H3O+.
Borax bead test: borax melts to sodium metaborate glass which dissolves transition-metal oxides to give colour.
Borax solution is alkaline and buffers near pH 9.2, which makes it useful in laundry applications.
Alums have the formula M(I)2SO4·M(III)2(SO4)3·24H2O and form large octahedral crystals.
Aluminium hydroxide formed by hydrolysis adsorbs impurities, which is the basis of water purification.
Aluminium chloride fumes in moist air because it hydrolyses to give hydrochloric acid.

items.text: Blue bead from cobalt with borax
items.note: Cobalt metaborate dissolves in the borax glass, giving the characteristic deep blue colour.
Al3+ hydrolyses to Al(OH)3, which coagulates the suspended clay and settles it out.

blocks.text: Pure silicon or germanium is an intrinsic semiconductor: every atom is bonded to four neighbours, all electrons are tied into covalent bonds at low temperature, and conductivity is slight. Raising the temperature breaks some bonds and releases electrons, so unlike a metal, a semiconductor conducts better when hot — the opposite temperature coefficient is the quick identification test. Doping changes everything: adding a group 15 element such as phosphorus introduces a fifth valence electron that has no bonding partner and is free to move, giving n-type material with extra electrons; adding a group 13 element such as boron creates a vacancy, or hole, that acts as a positive charge carrier, giving p-type material. A junction of the two forms a diode that conducts in one direction and a transistor that amplifies, which is the foundation of electronics. Silicon’s other chemistry runs through the Si–O bond: silicones are synthetic polymers with an alternating silicon–oxygen backbone and organic side groups, giving them thermal stability and water repellence, while silicates range from discrete tetrahedra to the three-dimensional frameworks of quartz and feldspar.

items: Semiconductor conductivity rises with temperature; metal conductivity falls.
n-type doping adds donor electrons from a group 15 element; charge carriers are electrons.
p-type doping creates holes with a group 13 acceptor; charge carriers are positive holes.
A p–n junction conducts in one direction only, giving rectification.
Silicones are (SiR2O) polymers, thermally stable and hydrophobic, used as lubricants and sealants.
Silicate structures: discrete (SiO4^4−), chain (Si2O6^4−), sheet (Si2O5^2−) and framework (SiO2).

items.note: Five valence electrons give four bonds and one mobile electron, producing n-type material.

items.text: Silicone rubber on an oven dish
items.note: The Si–O backbone resists heat and the organic groups repel water.

items.meaning: Pure semiconductor whose conductivity comes from thermally released electrons.
Doped semiconductor with mobile electrons supplied by a group 15 dopant.
Doped semiconductor with mobile holes created by a group 13 dopant.
Polymer with an alternating silicon–oxygen backbone and organic side groups.

keyPoints: Group 13 has the configuration ns^2 np^1 and commonly shows +3.
Boron never expands its octet because it has no accessible d orbitals.
BF3 is a Lewis acid; BF6^3− does not form.
Aluminium is amphoteric and dissolves in both acids and excess alkali.
The inert-pair effect makes Tl(I) and Pb(II) more stable than their higher oxidation states.
Carbon’s small size and strong C–C bond give it unmatched catenation.
Diamond is a hard insulator; graphite is soft and conducting because of delocalised electrons.
Semiconductors conduct better when heated, opposite to metals.
n-type doping adds electrons, p-type doping creates holes; the junction forms diodes and transistors.
Silicones and silicates both rest on the strength of the silicon–oxygen bond.
examFocus: Anomalies earn marks: give the cause (missing d orbital, inert pair, small size) with the observation.
Structural questions need the bonding type stated first, then the property, then the use.
Semiconductor answers must name the carrier in each type and the direction of the temperature effect.
For group 13 oxidation states, say explicitly that poor shielding by d and f electrons stabilises the lower state.

vocabulary.meaning: Electron-pair acceptor, as boron trifluoride is.
Bonding between atoms of the same element to form chains and rings.
Reluctance of the outer s electrons to participate in bonding in heavy p-block elements.
Addition of a trace impurity to a semiconductor to create mobile carriers.
Absence of an electron in a bonding position, acting as a positive charge carrier.
Synthetic polymer with Si–O repeating units and organic side groups.
Double sulphate of a group 1 and a group 3 metal with twenty-four waters of crystallisation.
Silicate in which every oxygen is shared, giving a three-dimensional network such as quartz.
Material with intermediate conductivity that rises with temperature.
Product of a coordinate bond between a Lewis acid and a Lewis base.

questions.prompt: The general outer electronic configuration of the group 13 elements is:
questions.explanation: Boron, aluminium and the rest have one electron in the outer p sub-shell alongside a filled s sub-shell.

questions.prompt: Boron forms BF3 but not BF6^3− because:
options: Boron has no d orbitals of low energy available to expand its octet
The BF6^3− ion would be too soluble
questions.answer: Boron has no d orbitals of low energy available to expand its octet
questions.explanation: With only the 2s and 2p levels available, boron is limited to eight electrons around it.

questions.prompt: In an n-type semiconductor the charge carriers are produced by doping silicon with:
questions.explanation: A group 15 atom forms four bonds and leaves a fifth electron free to move through the lattice.

questions.prompt: The increasing stability of the +1 oxidation state down group 13 is called:
questions.explanation: Poor shielding by the d and f electrons leaves the outer s pair held tightly and reluctant to bond.

questions.prompt: The ability of an element to form bonds with atoms of the same element, producing long chains, is called __________ .
questions.explanation: Catenation is strongest in carbon because of its small size and strong C–C bond.

questions.prompt: Boron trifluoride acts as a Lewis __________ because the boron atom has only six electrons around it.
questions.explanation: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair, which BF3 does to complete boron’s octet.

questions.prompt: Explain why aluminium oxide dissolves in both hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
questions.answer: Aluminium is a metal near the staircase, so Al2O3 has both basic and acidic character. With acid it acts as a base, forming aluminium salt and water; with alkali it acts as an acid, forming the soluble aluminate ion and water. An oxide that reacts with both is amphoteric.
questions.explanation: Intermediate metallic character gives intermediate oxide character.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between diamond and graphite in terms of structure and conductivity.
questions.answer: Diamond has every carbon bonded to four others in a rigid sp3 tetrahedral network with no free electrons, so it is extremely hard and does not conduct. Graphite has layers of sp2 carbon with three bonds each and one delocalised electron per atom, so it is soft, slippery and conducts electricity along the layers.
questions.explanation: Bonding sets both the mechanical and the electrical behaviour in each allotrope.

questions.prompt: Describe the preparation and structure of diborane and explain why it is described as electron-deficient.
questions.answer: Diborane is prepared by treating boron trifluoride with sodium hydride. Its molecule B2H6 has four terminal hydrogens forming normal two-centre two-electron B–H bonds in two planes, but the remaining two hydrogens form bridging B–H–B bonds using only two electrons shared across three atoms. Boron has only three valence electrons each, so six valence electrons cannot provide a conventional bond between each pair of atoms; the bridge bonds are therefore three-centre two-electron bonds, and the molecule is electron-deficient because it lacks enough electrons for ordinary two-centron bonding throughout.
questions.explanation: Count the available electrons: twelve from four terminal hydrogens’ worth of bonding leaves the bridge to be explained by delocalised three-centre bonds.

questions.prompt: Predict the products when lead(IV) oxide is heated with concentrated hydrochloric acid, and explain what the result says about lead’s oxidation states.
questions.answer: Lead(IV) oxide oxidises concentrated hydrochloric acid, being itself reduced to lead(II) chloride while chlorine gas is evolved: PbO2 + 4HCl → PbCl2 + Cl2 + 2H2O. The yellow-brown chlorine gas is identified by its smell and by discharging moist starch-iodide paper. The result shows that lead(IV) is a strong oxidising agent and that the +2 state is the stable one for lead, because the 6s^2 pair is poorly shielded and does not take part in bonding, which is the inert-pair effect in group 14.
questions.explanation: An oxidising agent is reduced itself; the stable product state reveals which oxidation state the inert pair favours.
